title: How do you secure REST APIs (HTTPS, JWT/OAuth2, input validation, rate limiting, RBAC/scopes, hide secrets, logging/auditing)?
shortTitle: How do you secure REST APIs
keyPoints: HTTPS encrypts data in transit with TLS; enforce it everywhere with redirects and HSTS.
JWT/OAuth2 authentication verifies identity with a signed token carrying claims like subject and roles.
RBAC and OAuth2 scopes enforce what an authenticated user may do; failures return 403 Forbidden.
Input validation with bean validation annotations on request DTOs rejects malformed data at the boundary.
Rate limiting caps requests per client and returns 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header.
Secrets come from environment variables or Vault, never hardcoded; audit logs record who did what without leaking tokens or passwords.

s1_definition.oneliner: Secure a REST API with layered defences: HTTPS, JWT/OAuth2 authentication, RBAC/scope authorization, input validation, rate limiting, secret management, and audit logging that never leaks secrets.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **HTTPS** – encrypts all data in transit with TLS; enforced with redirects and HSTS so credentials and tokens cannot be sniffed.
- **JWT/OAuth2** – authentication proving identity via a signed token the client sends as a `Bearer` token; the server verifies signature, expiry, issuer, and audience.
- **RBAC/Scopes** – authorization enforcing what an authenticated user may do, using roles (`ADMIN`, `CUSTOMER`) or OAuth2 scopes (`transfers:write`).
- **Input validation** – `@NotBlank`, `@DecimalMin` on request DTOs plus parameterized queries to reject malformed and malicious data.
- **Rate limiting** – caps requests per client per window; returns `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After` header.
- **Secret management** – credentials from environment variables or Vault, never in code; audit logs mask passwords and tokens.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of protecting National Bank of India's vault. HTTPS is the armoured pipe money travels through. The JWT token is Rajesh's ID badge. Role-based access is the rule that only managers enter the vault room. Input validation is the guard checking every form for forged entries. Rate limiting is the turnstile stopping a thousand PIN guesses per minute. Secret management is keeping the master keys in a locked safe, never taped to the wall. Logging is the CCTV recording who did what, without filming anyone's PIN.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Defence-in-Depth Layers:

  Client ─── HTTPS (TLS) ───→ API Gateway
                                  │
                            Rate Limiting (429)
                                  │
                            JWT Validation
                            (signature, expiry)
                                  │
                            RBAC / Scopes (403)
                                  │
                            Input Validation
                            (@NotBlank, parameterized queries)
                                  │
                            Service Logic
                                  │
                            Audit Logging
                            (who, what, when, outcome)
                                  │
                            Secret Management
                            (Vault / env vars)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Securing a REST API is defence in depth across seven complementary layers. HTTPS encrypts data in transit so tokens and account data cannot be sniffed. JWT/OAuth2 authentication proves identity with a signed token carrying claims. RBAC and scopes enforce permissions so an authenticated user only does what their role allows. Input validation rejects malformed data at the boundary with bean validation on request DTOs and parameterized queries. Rate limiting caps requests per client and returns 429 with Retry-After. Secret management keeps signing keys and database passwords out of code. Audit logging records who did what without ever writing passwords or tokens.

At National Bank of India, each layer earned its place. A token was sniffed on a cafe network because a test endpoint leaked over plain HTTP. A customer guessed the admin fraud report URL because there was no authorization check. A script tried thousands of login attempts before rate limiting was added. And a token was once found written to a log file.

The mindset is defence in depth: HTTPS protects the wire but not a stolen token, so short token lifetimes limit that damage. Validation stops injection but not an authorized user abusing their rights, so least-privilege scopes limit that. Each layer compensates for the others' blind spots.

Remember one sentence: secure the API in seven layers, because no single control is enough and each one covers a gap the others miss.
